items.title: Climate crisis gave Cheltenham a major headache – and more pain is coming
items.summary:
There is little the track’s bosses could have done to prevent the chaos on and off the track this weekend

Even after two days of racing afflicted by dozens of non-runners due to the fast ground, the elements still had not quite finished with Cheltenham on Sunday, when the third day of the track’s November meeting went ahead only after a late inspection – to assess standing water on the course after several hours of rain.

A crowd of more than 10,000 racegoers, swelled by a big contingent of students from the specialist racing events organiser INVADES, had largely assembled when the inspection was announced, and while the course was passed fit for racing 15 minutes later, it was another uncomfortable moment for all concerned at the end of a tricky three days in the west country.

An emotional Rory McIlroy dedicated a record-equalling eighth Race to Dubai title to his father, Gerry, who is recovering from major surgery in the United States. McIlroy was reduced to tears when recalling the parting message from McIlroy Sr as he headed for the closing events in the DP World Tour’s season.

McIlroy’s final round of 67 at the DP World Tour Championship in Dubai helped him to finish in second place, which was sufficient to edge out Eugenio Chacarra for the season-long order of merit crown. Tyrrell Hatton won the tournament itself, with Chacarra’s share of third meaning McIlroy prevailed by the narrow margin of 125 points. He later revealed Gerry had been at the forefront of his mind.

items.title: Record-breaking Andy Robertson is Scotland’s finest captain
items.summary:
As he passes Kenny Dalglish’s appearance total, it is important to remember that it is the left-back’s journey that sets him apart

Andy Robertson may not be Scotland’s greatest player, but he is indisputably their finest captain. It counts as sacrilege, even to generations who have watched Kenny Dalglish only on YouTube, to reputationally place Robertson above the Liverpool hero on the basis of a cap haul that will reach 103 in St Gallen on Monday. Dalglish’s international career ended at 102 and the curious events that meant he missed the 1986 World Cup.

There is no requirement to compare a left-back in 2026 to a forward from decades earlier. Dalglish and Robertson are men in different positions in essentially a different sport. Instead, Robertson’s march to the top of the cap pile gives cause to laud his contribution.

Continue reading...
items.t: Record-breaking Andy Robertson is Scotland’s finest captain

items.title: Banton’s century leads England to emphatic win in second ODI amid Australian soap opera
items.summary:
Australia’s sandpaper soap opera has become one of alternative facts, but recollections of the second game in this one-day international series are unlikely to differ too greatly. For Tom Banton and Gus Atkinson, architects of an emphatic 135-run victory for England under lights on Sunday it was a match to remember.

Banton was sublime after England were asked to bat, unfurling a crisp 121 from 99 balls to underpin an imposing total of 355 for six. No touring side had gone bigger against Australia in their own back yard – the ideal platform for Harry Brook’s pace attack to release the handbrake and level the three‑match series.

Seismic victory in Cardiff was cathartic and though Steve Tandy urges caution, maybe the ‘Welsh problem’ can be fixed

So that’s that fixed then. Wales are back and all is right with the world. Suddenly the dysfunction at the union, the financial plight, the disputes, the emptying stadiums, the defeats – oh, the defeats – feel a very long way away. The All Blacks have been beaten. The euphoria in the Principality Stadium, however many people were there – or more pertinently not – seemed as eerily familiar as it was cathartic. This was how Cardiff used to feel on match day.

items.title: Australia overpower New Zealand to win fourth consecutive men’s Rugby League World Cup
items.summary:
• Australia 32-12 New Zealand

  • Reece Walsh stars in dominant win for Kangaroos

The more things change, the more they stay the same. The past month has given us the rebirth of New ­Zealand as a legitimate top-tier force and the continuing rise of ­Pasifika rugby league with Samoa and Tonga – but in the end the one thing that really matters is the one thing that does not look like changing any time soon.

For the 10th time in the past 11 editions, the men’s Rugby League World Cup belongs to Australia. What we saw in Brisbane was not so much a surprise – the Kangaroos saving their best for when it really mattered – but more a disappointment, given the pre-match hype and the contest between these two on the opening night. That game four weeks ago was won by two points and although ­Australia looked below par and perhaps even slightly vulnerable in the tournament’s early moments, it was the Kiwis’ display which gave neutrals the greatest cause for optimism that a team could finally dethrone the Kangaroos. Perhaps this was finally the time, after England and Samoa failed in the past two finals.

items.t: Australia overpower New Zealand to win fourth consecutive men’s Rugby League World Cup

items.title: Terry Butcher: ‘I’ve learned to live with the Hand of God goal better’
items.summary:
The former England centre-back answers your questions on Diego Maradona, Bobby Robson and on staying in strange places

“Have you made up all these on your own?” asks Terry Butcher, sitting in a London office in the week he is presented with his England legacy cap. It turns out dozens of Guardian readers want to pick the brains of a much-loved centre-back who was feted en route to a World Cup semi-final and tormented four years previously by the mercurial genius of Diego Maradona.

Did Maradona ever admit to the “Hand of God”? Butcher found himself in the post-match doping-control room alongside his nemesis at the Azteca in 1986. “I tapped my head, then my hand, and then he tapped his head,” Butcher says. “He didn’t admit to it because, if he had, I’d have been right across that room.”

items.title: First-half blitz secures Australia’s fourth straight Women’s Rugby League World Cup title
items.summary:
• Jillaroos retain their crown with dominant 34-10 win over Kiwi Ferns

  • Jamie Chapman scores hat-trick before the break in Brisbane

In northern Australia, they call this time of the year “the build up” – a sub-tropical rise in heat and pressure where dark clouds roil and minds melt before the heavens open. At Brisbane’s Suncorp Stadium, it was Australia’s Jillaroos who brought the storm, dominating their New Zealand rivals from the get-go and raining down six first-half tries to win 34-10 and thunder their way to a fourth consecutive World Cup title.

If this Australian apocalypse had a horsewoman, it was star winger Jaime Chapman. The long-striding speedster scored three sensational tries in the first half alone to take her tournament tally to 13, breaking the record for an individual at a World Cup. Chapman already has 521,000 Instagram followers around the rugby-loving world. After this try-scoring spree – she now has 18 from her 10 Tests – it’ll be a million.

items.t: First-half blitz secures Australia’s fourth straight Women’s Rugby League World Cup title

items.title: Andreeva to face Svitolina in WTA Finals showpiece as Sabalenka apologises
items.summary:
• Russian teenager will face Ukrainian star in final

  • Sabalenka issues public apology after social media storm

The rise of Mirra Andreeva has seemed inevitable ever since she burst on to the tour as a precocious 15-year-old more than three years ago, but this week, six months after her maiden grand slam triumph at Roland Garros, she has taken another massive step forward in her career. The 19-year-old will attempt to close out the most impressive week of her career by winning one of her most significant titles after thoroughly outplaying Jessica Pegula, the fifth seed, 6-3, 6-4 to reach the championship match of the WTA Finals at the Indian Wells Tennis Garden.

A year ago, Andreeva surprisingly failed to qualify for the WTA Finals, missing out by a paltry six points after bizarrely deciding not to compete in the final tournament week before the event. The world No 3 has been utterly supreme in her long-awaited debut appearance, bulldozing through elite opposition to reach the final without dropping a set. She has conceded just 18 games in four matches this week, including a 6-4, 6-0 demolition of the No 1 seed Aryna Sabalenka, winning 11 games in succession from 1-4 down.

items.t: Andreeva sweeps past Pegula to reach WTA Finals title match after hot-mic controversy

items.title: Here Manchester United go again, taking the Two Ronnies route to hiring a new boss | Jonathan Wilson
items.summary:
Mauricio Pochettino’s arrival feels like yet another appointment that would have been better made a few years ago

Magnusson: And your time starts … now! What is paleontology? Smithers: Yes, absolutely correct. Magnusson: What’s the name of the directory that lists members of the peerage? Smithers: A study of old fossils. Magnusson: Correct. Who are Len Murray and Sir Geoffrey Howe? Smithers: Burke’s. Magnusson: Correct. What is the difference between a donkey and an ass? Smithers: One’s a trade union leader, the other’s a member of the Cabinet …

One of the Two Ronnies’ most celebrated sketches involves a Mastermind contestant whose specialist subject is answering the previous question. History repeats itself: the first time as comedy, the second time as Manchester United, who seem continually to be answering not the question of who would be the best available manager now, but who might have been the best available manager a few years ago.

items.title: England leave Jones sucking lemons but demolition of Japan shows widening gulf | Gerard Meagher
items.summary:
Brave Blossoms looked like Sunday afternoon amateurs but the one-sided result highlights the failings of the international landscape

What can we surmise from that? England are very good at shooting fish in a barrel. Max Ojomoh looks the part when given the freedom of Twickenham in which to operate. Will Joseph can finish, Maro Itoje can remove candy from the clutches of a baby and someone on the TV production crew has a sadistic streak.

After almost every England try – and there were 13 of them here – the camera would pan to Eddie Jones in the coaches’ box. His face that little more forlorn every time. One more lemon sucked. Japan had a man sent off before they had touched the ball and things got no better for the Brave Blossoms.

items.title: Mauricio Pochettino asked the US to believe in his project. Did he believe in it himself?
items.summary:
The coach’s tenure with the USMNT brought a whiplash of highs and lows. He met some goals but also left many with the impression he never truly bought in

It did not take US men’s national team coach Mauricio Pochettino very long to take his first big swing.

He’d just taken the reins of the program after a disastrous performance at the 2024 Copa América cost his predecessor his job, with the first home World Cup in three decades looming on the horizon. The federation introduced him in New York City, on the 24th floor of a building overlooking the Hudson River. In short order, he was asked about the culture surrounding the program. In his answer, he invoked the four-time World Cup champion US women.
